• The UK Home Office was reported to be continuing removals of asylum seekers to France under a “one in, one out” scheme despite its official end, raising legal and human-rights concerns.
• A federal judge dismissed Donald Trump’s defamation suit against the Wall Street Journal over a Jeffrey Epstein “birthday book” letter, ruling the complaint failed to show actual malice.
Why it matters: Social strains from inflation and governance concerns are fueling cross-border protest waves and contentious policy debates, while court rulings and migration practices continue to test institutions’ credibility.

Society & Human Rights.title: John Healey says UK apology over historic role in slave trade won’t lead to financial reparations – UK politics live
Society & Human Rights.text: Ahead of a meeting with Commonwealth leaders, Andy Burnham wrote that Britain needed to ‘acknowledge its complicated history’At the end of his interview with Kuennsberg, Healey was also asked to comment on a potential apology for Britain’s near-250 years of perpetrating the slave trade and why the government should or shouldn’t pay reparations to enslaved people and their countries.Sitting in the grand settings of Number 11 Downing St, Kuenssberg pointed out the lavish interiors:Considering a formal apology doesn’t mean accepting that British people now should accept the financial liability for any party and things that happened hundreds of years ago, in which they had no role.For almost 250 years (1560s-1807), British ships trafficked more than three million enslaved African men, women and children in a state policy backed by the monarchy and parliament.Many were taken to British-owned plantations in the Caribbean, which enslaved generations. Children were born into slavery, uprisings were put down with extreme brutalityThere were still 800,000 enslaved people on British plantations when enslavement was finally abolished by parliament in 1833U.K. politicians have traditionally focused on the country’s role in banning the slave trade in 1807 and outlawing slavery throughout the British Empire in 1833.Abolishment was only achieved because the government agreed to “compensate” the enslavers. The government paid an enormous sum, the equivalent of billions of dollars these days, to the “owners” of enslaved people; this came from a huge loan that was only paid off in 2015.Britain has never paid any compensation or reparations to the people who were enslaved, or their countries. Entertainment.text: SummaryJISOO has officially released her new solo single and accompanying music video for "ADDICTED"The dark dance-pop track explores the rush of magnetic attraction as an emotional parallel to her bond with fansThe release serves as the latest preview of her upcoming full-length solo album following her previous single "CLICK"BLACKPINK artist JISOO has officially released her new single "ADDICTED", delivering a moody dance-pop cut paired with an accompanying high-fashion music video. The track marks the latest preview of the BLACKPINK vocalist's forthcoming debut solo full-length album.Anchored by driving electronic rhythms, the single captures the intoxicating sensation of sudden attraction—a fleeting name, glance, or shared moment that lingers long after it passes. In a statement, her team explained that this romantic pull mirrors the enduring bond between JISOO and her listeners, transforming personal infatuation into a shared sentiment celebrating the anticipation of reuniting with what brings joy.The release builds directly upon the thematic groundwork laid by her previous single "CLICK," where a cinematic narrative cast JISOO as the sole sentient cyborg maintaining an abandoned theme park. Centered around the revitalizing bond between the protagonist and the symbolic "CLICK Bear"—a tribute to her global fanbase—the story emphasized unity across languages and borders. With "ADDICTED," JISOO pivots from futuristic whimsy to a sleek, nocturnal aesthetic, further expanding the visual and sonic world of her upcoming record.JISOO's new single "ADDICTED" and its accompanying music video are available now across streaming platforms.Read more at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Pas Normal Studios and Salomon Reunite for Sixth Technical Running Capsule
Entertainment.text: SummaryPas Normal Studios and Salomon have unveiled their sixth collaboration designed for cyclists transitioning into cold-weather runningThe three-piece collection introduces the waterproof AERO BLAZE 4 GRVL GORE-TEX alongside the GRAVEL CONCEPT 2 vest and S/LAB BELTThe collaborative technical capsule drops on November 5 across both brands' webstores flagships and select global retailersPas Normal Studios and Salomon have officially reunited for their sixth collaborative capsule, introducing a cold-weather running capsule headlined by the AERO BLAZE 4 GRVL GORE-TEX, the GRAVEL CONCEPT 2 vest, and the S/LAB BELT. Conceived specifically for the cyclist’s off-season transition into distance running, the three-piece lineup unites Scandinavian minimalism with alpine mountain performance.Anchoring the release is the AERO BLAZE 4 GRVL GORE-TEX, a versatile running shoe engineered for daily training across mixed terrains and unpredictable winter environments. The silhouette integrates Salomon’s signature lightweight cushioning and multi-surface traction with a fully waterproof GORE-TEX membrane for comprehensive weather resistance. Pas Normal Studios applies its refined color direction to the technical profile, establishing an aesthetic balance between high-output road and trail running and urban lifestyle versatility.The capsule is rounded out by two specialized storage solutions designed to maintain ergonomics during cold-weather movement. The GRAVEL CONCEPT 2 vest synthesizes Salomon’s proven expertise in stability, fit, and on-the-go hydration with a minimalist Nordic design language built for both daily routes and extended off-road exploration. Alongside the vest, the lightweight S/LAB BELT provides streamlined, bounce-free storage for essential gear. Highlighting the intersection of both endurance disciplines, Pas Normal Studios co-founder and creative director Karl-Oskar Olsen stated that the collection is designed to meet the demands of athletes seeking unexplored terrain during seasonal transitions.The Pas Normal Studios x Salomon collection releases on November 5, 2026, via PNS, Salomon, Pas Normal Studios flagship stores, and select global retail partners.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Palace and Burberry Announce Limited-Edition Capsule for London Flagship Opening
Entertainment.text: SummaryPalace and Burberry have announced a limited-edition 10-piece collaborative capsule celebrating the opening of Palace's new London flagshipThe lineup reinterprets the classic Camden car coat in honey beige alongside graphic tees hooded jackets caps skateboards and a hybrid Tri-Ferg Equestrian Knight logoThe collection launches on November 5 exclusively in person at Palace's new Soho flagship located at 8 Poland StreetPalace and Burberry have officially announced an exclusive collaborative collection, celebrating the opening of the London streetwear label's new flagship space. Uniting British heritage fashion with authentic skate culture, the 10-piece drop will be available exclusively at Palace’s new Soho location to commemorate the retail milestone.Leading the limited-edition lineup is Burberry’s signature Camden car coat, reworked in its original honey beige hue with countryside-inspired screen-printed artwork across the silhouette. The capsule expands across functional skate and casual wardrobe staples, encompassing hooded jackets, graphic tees, caps, and collaborative skateboards. Throughout the range, Burberry’s classic house check appears alongside a hybrid logo that blends Palace’s unmistakable Tri-Ferg emblem with Burberry’s heritage Equestrian Knight motif across select styles.The announcement lands at a defining transitional moment for Palace, which recently closed its long-standing Brewer Street location to make way for a larger, multi-floor flagship just around the corner at 8 Poland Street. Known for partnering with unexpected cultural powerhouses, the London skate imprint adds Burberry to its growing catalog of luxury collaborations, connecting high-end British tailoring directly with Soho street aesthetics.The Palace x Burberry capsule launches on November 5 exclusively at Palace’s new Soho flagship store located at 8 Poland Street in London. Sports.title: Golden State Valkyries Defeat Atlanta Dream in Game 7 to Capture Historic First WNBA Championship
Sports.text: SummaryThe Golden State Valkyries secured their first WNBA championship with a 68-63 Game 7 victory over the Atlanta DreamFinals MVP Gabby Williams scored 28 of her 30 points in the second half setting a new WNBA Finals record for points in a halfThe title comes in only the franchise's second season following previous collegiate and overseas championships for WilliamsThe Golden State Valkyries captured their first WNBA championship in franchise history after defeating the Atlanta Dream 68-63 in Game 7 of the WNBA Finals. The victory comes in just the franchise's second season, propelled by a historic 30-point performance from Finals MVP Gabby Williams.After trailing by six points entering the locker room at halftime, Golden State mounted a fierce second-half comeback orchestrated almost entirely by Williams. The 30-year-old star exploded for 28 of her 30 points in the final 20 minutes, breaking the WNBA Finals record for the most points scored in a single half. Williams notched 15 points in the third quarter alone, shifting the momentum and handing the Valkyries a 45-44 lead heading into the final frame.With the deciding contest locked at 53-53 in the fourth quarter, Williams took control down the stretch, scoring nine straight points for Golden State. Her run was punctuated by a deep 3-pointer with 2:18 remaining to establish a 60-57 advantage that the Valkyries protected through the final buzzer. In addition to her offensive heroics, the Defensive Player of the Year runner-up anchored Golden State on the opposite end of the floor with four blocks.The triumph marks Williams' first career WNBA title following previous stints in Chicago and Seattle. The milestone also provides an elusive championship breakthrough after heartbreaking one-point international defeats representing France at the 2024 Paris Olympic Games and the women's FIBA World Cup. Art & Culture.title: When Electric Cars Were for Women
Art & Culture.text: At the turn of the last century, the automobile industry was still new and evolving rapidly. In 1898, there were about 50 carmakers in the United States. A decade later, that number had increased fivefold. In 1901, the companies produced 7,000 vehicles. By 1910, production had reached 181,000.For several decades, electric cars vied with those powered by steam and internal combustion, and nobody was sure which technology would come out on top. Steam had the legacy of locomotive technology behind it but came with a risk of fire. Steam-powered vehicles could also become exceedingly hot, depending on the placement of the boiler and the steam piping. Both gasoline and electric cars faced logistical challenges: How far could you travel without refueling or charging? You could always throw an extra can of gasoline in the back of the car, but charging a battery involved more planning. The infrastructure for long-distance travel was not yet in place.Before the invention of the electric starter in 1911, gasoline-powered engines had to be started with a hand crank; once running, they were loud and emitted noxious fumes. Fully electric vehicles, by contrast, were easy to start; you just turned on the main battery switch, often with a key, and there was no foul exhaust to deal with. Electric carmakers looking for a way to differentiate their products decided that these attributes made their vehicles perfect for women. (Electric cars were also marketed to doctors so that they could make house calls in the middle of the night without waking the neighbors.) General Electric, which made car chargers based on mercury-arc rectifiers, was so captivated by the idea of women driving electric cars that the company created a series of advertisements featuring stylishly dressed women plugging in their cars and posing with their charging stations.  In ads for its electric car chargers, General Electric featured women using the equipment.miSci—Museum of Innovation and ScienceA young woman named Fannie Goodnow was an early EV adopter. She owned a 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton, an open two-seater that really did look like a horseless carriage, and she used a GE mercury-arc rectifier to charge it. Who Invented the Mercury-Arc Rectifier?  Electrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt invented the mercury vapor lamp, which became the basis for the mercury-arc rectifier used in car-charging systems. Bettmann/Getty ImagesElectrical engineer Peter Cooper Hewitt is generally credited with the invention of the mercury-arc rectifier. During the first decade of the 20th century, Hewitt received several U.S. patents for electric lamps and other apparatus for transmitting and using electric currents. U.S. patents 968,896 and 1,163,706, granted to Percy H. Thomas, advanced Hewitt’s designs. Thomas was chief electrician for the Cooper Hewitt Electric Co., which Hewitt had cofounded with George Westinghouse to manufacture and sell his lamps.The mercury-arc rectifier functioned as a diode. In a car charger like the one Fannie Goodnow used, it converted alternating current from the power grid into direct current needed to charge the car’s battery. A small amount of liquid mercury contained in a glass tube would vaporize and glow as electricity passed through it. Coupled with the carbon anodes, the vapor allowed current to flow in only one direction. This unit took about 12 hours to charge a drained battery. A Carriage Maker Pivots to Electric CarsI couldn’t find any records as to why Fannie Goodnow opted for an electric car. But as a well-to-do woman living in the Boston area, she had more than a half dozen automobile producers to choose from. The one she chose was S.R. Bailey & Co. of Amesbury, Mass.  This early electric car charger used a mercury-arc rectifier to convert AC to DC.Heritage Museums & GardensAccording to Galen Handy, who maintains the Early Electric Vehicles website, Samuel Robinson Bailey started in the carriage and sleigh business as a teenager, winning a best-in-show prize at a carriage exhibition in Portland, Maine, in 1855. Bailey developed a reputation as an inventor and designed processes to streamline the manufacture of his vehicles. He went into business for himself in 1882. Just over a decade later, one of Bailey’s carriages won a gold medal at the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.Bailey’s son Edwin attended the exposition, where he likely would have seen a vision of the future: the Morrison electric wagon. This six-passenger, battery-powered vehicle ferried visitors and VIPs around the fairgrounds. It wasn’t long before automobiles began eating into the carriage business. In December 1906, with the carriage industry collapsing, S.R. Bailey & Co. announced it was getting into electric vehicles.Thomas Edison Designed a Bad BatteryBailey’s first model, the Victoria Phaeton, used an Edison alkaline battery. Thomas Edison had been working on a lighter, more reliable, and more powerful battery for the auto industry since the 1890s, and announced the achievement with great fanfare in 1903. Unfortunately for Bailey and other carmakers who deployed it, the battery leaked and wouldn’t hold a charge. Edison was forced to go back to the drawing board. By 1910, he had a better battery in production, but by then his friend Henry Ford had introduced the Model T, setting the stage for the internal combustion engine to take over the market.While Edison toiled to improve his tech, Bailey pivoted to a battery from the Gould Storage Battery Co. of Depew, N.Y. Gould also supplied batteries for railroads, utilities, subways, elevators, and farms. Goodnow’s Victoria Phaeton used a 30-cell lead-acid battery housed in a wooden box that was suspended under the chassis. The standard battery had a range of 64 to 80 kilometers; a larger battery with 50 percent more capacity was available for an upcharge. With the standard battery, the Victoria Phaeton cost US $2,000 (about $73,000 today, or about the list price of an upscale EV like the Audi Q8 or BMW i5).  Fannie Goodnow’s electric car charger now resides at the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. But her 1908 Bailey Victoria Phaeton has been lost to history. Shown here is a 1911 version of that model.Sarah Thornington/Heritage Museums & GardensGoodnow installed a mercury-arc rectifier charging station in the barn adjacent to her parents’ summer home in Hull, Mass. Bill Lillie of Vintage Electric Cars notes that the charging plug was of an unusual design. This is, of course, one of the banes of any early adopter: nonstandardized plugs and cables. The Electric Vehicle Association of America, which formed in 1910, tried to put forward a standard so that electric vehicles could be charged at any charging station. (Modern EV owners can no doubt relate.) But savvy electric car owners knew to carry spare plug adapters and cables when traveling.When Edison’s improved battery was finally available, Bailey began using it in the Victoria Phaeton and then went on a publicity blitz. In September 1910, the carmaker sponsored a round-trip tour from New York to Boston, with a side trip up New Hampshire’s Mount Washington, totaling about 1,600 km. Sadly, the “This Car Climbed Mt. Washington” bumper sticker hadn’t yet become popular.   Thomas Edison supplied the batteries for an electric car made by S.R. Bailey & Co., which then went on a publicity road trip from New York to Boston. miSci—Museum of Innovation and ScienceAlthough Thomas Edison posed for a photo with the new Bailey Victoria Phaeton that featured his new battery, he himself chose a Detroit Electric Victoria for his own use. (Edison was known to be a terrible driver, so someone else likely chauffeured him around.) Unable to compete against the rising tide of Model Ts, S.R. Bailey sold its factory in 1915, having produced about 500 to 600 electric vehicles.Although the vehicle Fannie Goodnow chose turned out to be just a blip in automotive history, I like to imagine her driving about town in a beautiful car that embodied all the quirks of early adoption. I hope her friends didn’t make fun of her for investing in electric just before internal combustion took off. I hope she didn’t get stranded without the proper charging cable. I do not know what happened to her or her Victoria Phaeton, but her charging station remained in situ until 2022, when it was donated to the Heritage Museums & Gardens in Sandwich, Mass. Now it stands ready to tell stories of technological change and adoption that continue to resonate today.Part of a continuing series looking at historical artifacts that embrace the boundless potential of technology.An abridged version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue.ReferencesFor a detailed history of the development of the mercury-arc rectifier (or valve), see Deepak Tiku’s article in the March/April 2014 issue of IEEE Power & Energy Magazine.Harry Cooke Cushing Jr., a fellow of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers, wrote (and updated regularly over a number of years) The Electric Vehicle Hand-Book, which gave general instructions for the care and storage of batteries, including how to charge them with a mercury-arc rectifier. Discussion of the mercury-arc rectifier begins on page 156 of the 10th edition, published in 1922. (The American Institute of Electrical Engineers is one of the predecessor organizations of the IEEE.)
